soil-bio-300.title: Living, active and passive: three kinds of organic matter
soil-bio-300.text:
Soil organic matter is usefully split into living, active (dead) and passive (very dead, humus) parts, and each serves a different role. Living matter is roots and organisms in spaces between and inside larger aggregates. Active matter is fresh or partly decomposed residue in the same spaces. Passive matter is fragments of dead microbes held on clay and silt, residue inside micro-aggregates, and compounds hard for organisms to use.

A soil needs active matter as well as humus. It supplies nutrients, aggregating glues and food for diverse organisms. It is also the part that suffers first. Early losses after cultivating forest or grassland were nearly all the unprotected active part, and that part rises fastest with reduced tillage, rotation, cover crops, manure and compost. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-293.title: How soil protects its organic matter
soil-bio-293.text:
Organic matter persists in soil through chemical bonding to clay, physical protection in aggregates and conversion to stable humic substances. Aggregates matter most here. Large aggregates are built from smaller ones held by sticky substances from roots, bacterial colonies and fungal hyphae.

Matter outside small aggregates, and free particulate matter, is available to organisms. Use also needs a favourable chemical form, location, moisture and aeration. Compaction, dense layers or low spots with poor aeration slow use. Protection is therefore partly a matter of where the matter sits, as well as what it is. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-309.title: Why some crop residues last and others vanish
soil-bio-309.text:
Only about 10-20% of a residue is converted to stable humus after decomposition. How fast it goes, and what it leaves, depends on its chemistry. Residues low in hemicellulose, polyphenols and {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, such as green legume cover crops and soybean residue, decompose fast. Their effect on organic matter is shorter than that of cornstalks or wheat straw. Manure with much bedding decomposes slowly and lasts longer in soil, and ruminant manure lasts longer than that of grain-fed chickens and hogs.

Easily decomposed residues, manures, cover crops and straw boost aggregation more than compost, which has already decomposed, though compost raises water-holding capacity. A variety of residues is needed to feed diverse organisms, supply nutrients and promote aggregation. Lignin-rich straw or sawdust builds organic matter but needs added nitrogen. Otherwise the microbes run short and less becomes humus. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-304.title: Filling the soil's organic matter sites
soil-bio-304.text:
When practices change to favour buildup, organic matter fills protected sites first and then accumulates mainly as free particles until the soil reaches equilibrium. Free mineral surfaces bond with organic matter first. Small aggregates then form around organic particles, and larger aggregates follow, held by mycorrhizal fungi and small roots.

Once all bonding sites and small-aggregate sites are filled, the soil is saturated for that management. Extra organic matter stays as lightly protected free particles that decompose fairly quickly. Depleting practices reverse the order: free particles go first, then aggregate-protected matter, leaving matter tightly held on clay and in micro-aggregates.

So a depleted soil can gain much more than one already full for its texture and drainage. With clay and poor aeration, upkeep needs less residue than in well-aerated coarse sands, where raising it is hardest. Case 1 degraded soils and case 2 suboptimal soils gain most from carbon farming. Nearly full case 3 soils should protect what they have, perhaps exporting surplus manure to grain farms. The protection itself is described in {{ref:soil-bio-293}}, and the three pools in {{ref:soil-bio-300}}.

soil-bio-306.title: A simple model of equilibrium organic matter
soil-bio-306.text:
A simple model sets a soil's equilibrium organic matter from two numbers: the annual residue addition and the annual decomposition rate. Add 5,000 pounds of residue yearly to a sandy loam decomposing 3% a year, and equilibrium is about 1.7%. Add 7,500 pounds yearly to a well-drained coarse soil decomposing 5% a year, and equilibrium is only about 1.5%. More residue does not help if decomposition is faster.

The approach is gradual. The 5,000-pound case, starting at 1%, nets about 350 pounds per acre per year in the first decade, falling toward zero as steady state nears. A very depleted soil starting at 0.5% might gain over 600 pounds per acre per year initially because protective sites are open, so it rises faster. Annual changes are tens to hundreds of pounds against 20,000 pounds per percent, so changes take years to detect. The idea of open sites comes from {{ref:soil-bio-304}}.

soil-bio-316.title: How minerals lock organic matter away for centuries
soil-bio-316.text:
Organic matter can persist for decades to centuries. It does so largely because it binds to minerals and is physically protected inside aggregates. {{ref:soil-chem-079}} bind organic matter by covalent, ionic or van der Waals interactions, making it hard for microbes to reach. Iron and aluminium oxides do this in acidic soils. In neutral and alkaline soils, calcium and magnesium bridges link organic molecules to clay. 2:1 clays with higher surface area adsorb more carbon than 1:1 clays.

Inside aggregates, organic matter is spatially separated from decomposers and has less oxygen, as described in {{ref:soil-bio-293}}. One form of carbon needs no such shelter. Pyrogenic carbon from boreal fires, with condensed aromatic structures, can persist as a long-term sink, though persistence varies with formation conditions.

soil-bio-286.title: Organic matter and the nitrogen cycle
soil-bio-286.text:
Each percent of organic matter in the top 6 inches holds about 1,000 pounds of nitrogen. Almost all soil nitrogen is part of organic matter, in forms plants cannot use directly. Plants take up most of theirs as nitrate and a little as ammonium, and small amounts of amino acids and small proteins can also be absorbed. Each year bacteria and fungi convert some organic nitrogen to ammonium and other bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate. A crop may draw 20-50% of its nitrogen from mineralized organic matter.

Other sources are manure, nitrogen-fixing bacteria (large amounts under legumes), rain and snow deposition, and industrially fixed fertilizer, the largest addition for most grain crops.

Losses follow. Nitrate leaches readily, especially from sandy and tile-drained soils, reaching groundwater or causing dead zones. Uncomposted manure or surface fertilizer may lose up to 30% by volatilization. Denitrification by bacteria in saturated soils turns nitrate into N2 and nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas estimated as agriculture's largest greenhouse contribution that also thins the ozone layer. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-hist-034.title: Rethinking what soil organic matter is
soil-hist-034.text:
Historically, stability was blamed on humic substances, formed from inputs and extracted with strong base and acid, then interpreted as large stable macromolecules. From the late 1990s high-resolution chemistry showed that {{ref:soil-found-045}} is recognizable plant and animal biomolecules at varying degradation stages, which can associate like larger molecules. Flaws in the old view showed in 1999, when soil models could not account for the large charcoal component of Chernozems.

A newer paradigm holds that molecular structure alone does not explain persistence. Microbial carbon-use efficiency matters, and labile molecules taken up by microbes may form most stable organic matter. The debate is live. The {{ref:soil-chem-063}} still appears in textbooks while some researchers argue it is wrong. Compare {{ref:soil-bio-090}} and the {{ref:soil-bio-092}}.

soil-bio-294.title: The soil organic matter balance
soil-bio-294.text: The amount of organic matter in a soil is the net result of all additions and losses over the years. If additions exceed losses it rises, as in natural soil formation. If losses exceed additions it falls, as generally when soils enter crop production. If they are equal it holds steady. Residue additions raise it, while faster decomposition or erosion deplete it. Tillage, rotation and manuring all strongly affect it. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-295.title: What cropping costs a soil's organic matter
soil-bio-295.text:
A Vermont clay soil lost 20% of its organic matter in five years of silage corn after decades of sod. Many Midwest soils lost 50% within 40 years of cropping. Converting grassland or forest to cropland sharply cuts soil organic matter through less residue returned, plowing-accelerated mineralization and erosion. Cash grain systems export 55-60% of organic matter even with residue retention.

Loss is rapid in early years because active organic matter is plentiful, then slows as mainly stable material remains. In Canada, converting native land to cropland cost about 25% of the carbon in the top 30 cm, about 1 Pg of emissions from 19th-century grassland soils. Most of the loss came in the first twenty years. Deep tall-grass prairie soils kept their productivity long because they began with unusually high organic matter and nutrient reserves.

Increased decomposition, not erosion, is typically the main culprit, as tillage breaks aggregates and exposes organic matter. The loss is mostly the light fraction of partly decomposed young residues. Residue removal, erosion, and sometimes fire used to clear land added to it. The starting point is the {{ref:soil-bio-294}}.

soil-bio-307.title: Managing the turnover of soil organic matter
soil-bio-307.text: Organic matter decomposes in all soils, so good management continually supplies new organic matter to feed organisms and replace what is lost. Minimize soil disturbance to keep aggregates and the organic matter inside them. Keep the surface covered with living plants or cover crops, or with residue mulch. Use rotations with perennials, cover crops and extensive-rooted crops, and add composts, manures or other off-field organic materials. The logic follows the {{ref:soil-bio-294}}.

soil-bio-301.title: How management shifts the living soil
soil-bio-301.text: The weight of living organisms in soil differs with vegetation and cropping system. Fungi outweigh bacteria in forest soils, roughly equal them in grasslands, and weigh less than bacteria in routinely tilled soils. Organisms are more abundant and diverse under complex rotations with diverse residues, cover crops, manures and composts, but frequent cultivation depletes their food. Compaction removes large pores first. A 1 mm pore is large and root tips are about 0.1 mm wide, so fewer earthworms, beetles, mites and springtails survive in compacted soil. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-302.title: How much organic matter is enough
soil-bio-302.text: Two percent organic matter is very good for a sandy soil but marks severe depletion in a clay soil. There are few accepted guidelines for adequate organic matter, and the right level depends strongly on texture and erosion risk. Fine mineral particles can saturate: a soil with 20% silt and clay can store at most about 3.6%, and one with 80% about 6.1%, excluding particulate organic matter. Total organic matter changes slowly, but an active-fraction test is more sensitive and gives an early sign of improvement. Sloping, erodible or already eroded soils need more organic input than level land. See {{ref:soil-found-045}} and {{ref:soil-found-051}}.
